cells.tense: You're in the middle of the work with your own hands on it.
cells.ask: Take one thing you've been carrying past its finish — the pile by the door, the project on its last step — and spend ten minutes telling someone what those hours were for and who is better off with it done. What you pick up next starts from a full tank.
cells.core:
The work is in your hands today and you're in it. You can tell when something in your care is finished and when it still needs you, and letting the finished ones go is ordinary for you. People feel the difference between what you hold loosely and what you're still carrying, even when nobody says so.

What that holding costs stays invisible until someone looks. The thing you've been tending past its finish is still taking your hours, and saying out loud what those hours bought and who they were for puts the truth of it on the table. Ten minutes of that can't be taken back, and it's how the weight comes off your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's finished and what isn't — and you let the finished ones go.
cells.verb: tending what is still growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: the point where what has been built is finished and handed on

cells.tense: You're standing in this week with one eye on the day it will all be done right.
cells.ask: Pick the earliest step you can actually reach — today, maybe tonight — and carry that one step all the way to done before you touch the next thing. One complete piece, said in your own words, and the finished feeling arrives on the far side of that step instead of down the road.
cells.core:
The week in front of you is real, but most of your attention is on the day it will all be done right. Whatever is in your hands gets tended for the version of it that hasn't arrived, and the piece you finish today doesn't quite count as finished.

A day's step can be carried to the end and set down the way a day's work gets set down. Giving one step the whole of today's attention, no further than that, brings the finished feeling back inside reach, and the week you're actually living in gets more solid under your feet.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding this week together and watching next year at the same time.
cells.verb: tending what is still growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: the point where what has been built is finished and handed on

cells.tense: There's a corner of your life waiting to be picked up, and you've stopped expecting much from picking it up.
cells.ask: Choose one small thing that asks something of you — a plant, a shelf, a page of notes — and give it ten minutes before the day crowds in. Keep to only what you can see yourself finish, and one small thing kept alive starts the rest of it moving.
cells.core:
The things you'd once have tended are sitting where they are, and you don't expect much from starting again. You watch other people's finished work from a distance. What's around you isn't finished enough to stand on, so it stays as it is.

A shelf can be cleared in ten minutes on an ordinary morning. One small thing tended where you can see it — watered, put in order, cleared off — is the whole step, and stopping at the piece you can finish means the doing starts working on you while you do it. Dependability wasn't what was missing, so the beginning can stay this small.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped expecting much from what you'd tend, and nothing around you is finished enough to say otherwise.
cells.verb: tending what is still growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: the point where what has been built is finished and handed on

cells.tense: Keeping your people fed and steady is something you handle, and you give it no weight.
cells.ask: Admit one thing you've been doing because it mattered — said once to one person, or written down where you'll see it — and let it count as the work it is. What you carry is already visible; letting yourself be seen near it is what's left.
cells.core:
Feeding your people and keeping them steady is something you do, and you file it under nothing much. You handle the plain part: the food, the accounts, the promise kept on the day it was promised. Other people can name what it holds up, and the one doing it says nothing about it.

This kind of work does its largest part on ordinary days, in a household kept running without announcement. Admitting one piece of it — what you carry and why you carry it — puts the doing back in your own hands, and the credit lands where the doing happens.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding this together and calling it nothing.
cells.verb: tending what is still growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: the point where what has been built is finished and handed on

attempts.check: The draft keeps every claim inside the four records: tending, holding two things at once, completion, and the wording of the four medicines. A reader could reasonably object that tending and finishing are common to everyone, so each cell names a gym, a shelf, a review or a group of people before it says anything about the person. Each ask survives being wrong: it stands on a chosen object, a first skim, a ten-minute beginning, a spoken admission, all observable and all giving something back whichever status the person is actually in. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is the Too Much seedbed line, and the closing word 'praised' is cut from it.
